(Read from the full embedded in the Internet Archive the Internet Archive capture, 2026-08-13, of the author's academia.edu upload, item 37130991.) Second source: Post, Mark W. 2015. Tones in Northeast Indian languages, with a focus on Tani: A fieldworker's guide. In Post, Morey & DeLancey (eds.), Language and Culture in Northeast India and Beyond, 182-210. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics.
catalog_locator: Modi 2017, ch. 2 Phonology, subsection 'Prosody (tone and stress)', p. 103 (running header '2. PHONOLOGY 103'; text extract, char offset 198529; TOC entry at offset ~20954). Post 2015, section 3 'Tone in Tani languages', pp. 188-189 (pp. 216-217 of the APL volume) and Table 5.
catalog_quote: Prosody (tone and stress) Although it seems that Milang is most likely a tone language, unfortunately I have been unable to analyse the tone system of Milang up to date. Work on tone in Milang is difficult because even native speakers are not aware of the tones, and sometimes realize them in different ways. This is similar to what Post (2015b) describes for Eastern Tani languages. Similarly for stress. I hope that in the future it will be possible to analyse the prosody system of Milang.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only full grammar of Milang (by a native-speaker linguist) explicitly leaves prosody unanalysed: Milang is probably tonal (Post 2015 adds: tone apparently layered with register/voice quality), but neither the tone system nor stress has been worked out; no statement of where word stress falls exists in the description.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the thesis elsewhere treats vowel length (incl. 'vowel length for emphatic purpose', pp. 90-92) and irregular syllable reduction (pp. 101-103) but never ties them to stress.
new_statements.domain_note: No domain specified; the author treats tone and stress jointly under 'prosody' and defers both to future work. Post 2015 (pp. 188-189, saved PDF) independently confirms Milang tone is undocumented.
new_statements.identity_note: Modi 2017 describes Milang (autonym area Holon; villages Milang/Holon, Dalbing, Peki Modi, Upper Siang district), glottocode mila1245, no ISO 639-3 code; the author is a native-speaker linguist and notes dialect mixing with Padam (Adi) in newer settlements. Post 2015's remark refers to the same language.

tone_statements.citation: Modi, Yankee. 2015. Towards an understanding of language distribution in the Tani area: Social organization, expansion and migration. In Mark W. Post, Stephen Morey & Scott DeLancey (eds.), Language and Culture in Northeast India and Beyond: In Honor of Robbins Burling (Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 23), 245-264. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: And it is in this area that we find what may be the simplest form of Tani language – tones have been lost completely, there are few evidential particles, complex person-sensitive TAME systems (i.e. ‘conjunct-disjunct’ marking) are gone ... On the other hand Milang, whose speakers have long inhabited a mountainous cul-de-sac on the northeastern extreme of the Tani area, has a complex tone + voice system, complex person-sensitive alternations, and an extremely large system of particles with an especially wide range of information-status functions even by Tani standards.
tone_statements.locator: p. 261, ch. 14, section 4 (linguistic consequences), paragraph contrasting Padam and Milang
tone_statements.summary: Tonal, 'complex tone + voice (phonation) system'; inventory not stated.
